summary: Authors from Carleton University and Cisco model OpenAI Agents SDK multi-agent workflows as typed graphs of agents, allowed and restricted tool edges, and delegation edges. From each graph they derive coverage obligations, then use DSPy with gpt-4.1-mini and a 5-attempt, runtime-grounded refine loop to write natural-language scenarios that should exercise each obligation. On ten SDK-derived demo workflows (403 obligations, mocked tools, single run), the body reports 45/65 allowed-tool and 31/41 delegation edges witnessed, and 23/248 restricted-tool call attempts elicited. There is no baseline generator, no mutation analysis, and no released code.

claims.claim: Generated scenarios witness 54/75 allowed-tool obligations and 36/48 delegation obligations
claims.evidence: These numbers appear only in the abstract and §I. Table I totals are 65 allowed and 41 delegation edges, and Table II, §IV-E and the RQ2 summary all report 45/65 (69.2%) and 31/41 (75.6%). The abstract figures do not appear anywhere in the results.
claims.location: Abstract, §I vs Table I, Table II, §IV-E

claims.claim: The restricted-tool criterion elicits 23/248 violations, separating workflows whose restrictions hold from workflows with concrete misrouting failures
claims.evidence: Table II sums to 23/248. However, in every benchmark the 'restricted' set is exactly agents x tools minus allowed edges (e.g. octagon 12x12-12=132; financial 7x7-7=42), which contradicts §II's rule that undeclared pairs are 'unspecified'. The SDK has no restriction declarations, and the adapter registers restricted tools as recording stubs. So a 'violation' is an attempt that production SDK wiring would likely make impossible. Results are single-run, and a zero count is not evidence of safety.

claims.claim: Structural coverage is a useful adequacy layer that end-to-end task evaluation misses
claims.evidence: No existing test suite or benchmark is measured for structural coverage. There is no mutation analysis to show that covered suites catch workflow regressions (deferred to future work, §VI), and no random or unguided generator for comparison.

claims.claim: Topology drives misses: single-hop targets pass, multi-hop and overlapping-specialist targets fail
claims.evidence: Table II regimes: single-hop 7/7 allowed-tool and fan-out coordinators 19/23. Misses fall on 2-hop targets in ydmitry and on handoff stubs in value_investment. Single run with one model.

claims.claim: Runtime-grounded DSPy refinement makes generation coverage-driven rather than prompt-driven
claims.evidence: Support is one worked trace (Fig. 3, four attempts). There is no ablation without refinement. The routing-prompt 'ablation' (Table III) is 2/2 vs 2/2 on one workflow. Fault injection (Table V) is 2/2 per mode.

patterns.note: Treats a developer-declared workflow graph (agents, tool edges, handoff edges) as a testable artifact and derives per-edge coverage obligations. On the DAG question, the declared edges here are routed by the LLM, and they are not reliably followed: 10/41 delegations and 20/65 allowed-tool edges went unexercised within 5 tries, and agents attempted off-edge tools 23/248 times when the adapter exposed them. No comparison is made with a different generator or with code-routed transitions. Single run, one model.
Multi-agent handoff and Agent.as_tool topologies are the object under test. There is no team-vs-single comparison.

Uses a closed-world tool-access model. The ~9% attempted restricted calls, when tools were visible, suggest that role or prompt restrictions leak, which argues for deterministic allowlists. No enforced-allowlist arm is measured.
Uses an execution-grounded binary reward (run the scenario, check the trace) to refine test scenarios. No ablation against generation without that feedback.
Witnesses are computed mechanically from runtime traces of agents, tools and handoffs, deliberately without an LLM judge.
Argues that task-success benchmarks miss structural coverage, but does not measure it.

methodology.sample: 10 OpenAI Agents SDK-derived workflows (official examples plus third-party demo or research projects): 49 reachable agents, 47 tools, 403 obligations. oai_customer_service serves as the instrumented case.
methodology.baselines: None. No random or unguided scenario generator, no measurement of existing tests or end-to-end benchmarks; the routing-prompt ablation is 2/2 vs 2/2.
methodology.models: gpt-4.1-mini for both the DSPy realizer and every agent under test
methodology.variance: Single run per benchmark; none reported
methodology.ablations: Strict vs loose routing prompt on one workflow (no difference); two tool-fault modes on one workflow (2/2 each)

standards.artifacts: No code, extracted manifests or generated scenarios released (no repository link); subject workflows are public

biases.detail: Abstract and introduction report 54/75 allowed-tool and 36/48 delegation witnesses. The body tables report 45/65 and 31/41, against totals of 65 and 41 edges.

Restricted edges are the full complement of allowed edges rather than developer declarations, and restricted tools are exposed as stubs by the test adapter. 'Violations' therefore measure the LLM's willingness to call a visible but undeclared tool, not a failure of the real workflow.
The authors' generator is scored by the authors' coverage criteria, with no external adequacy signal such as mutation detection.
gpt-4.1-mini plays both test generator and system under test.
All runtime results are single runs (acknowledged).
Most workflows are demo-scale, and tool backends are mocked.
One Python framework only; the extractor and adapter are SDK-specific.
Index terms list 'mutation analysis', but no mutation analysis is performed (deferred to future work).

coi.affiliations: Carleton University; second author at Cisco Systems
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: OpenAI Agents SDK example workflows and third-party projects built on it (not a Cisco product)
coi.detail: One author has a vendor affiliation, but no product of that vendor is evaluated or promoted.

verdict_reason: The coverage model is clearly specified, and the body tables are internally consistent. The abstract's headline witness counts do not match the body, though. The restricted-tool 'violations' are an artifact of complement-derived restrictions and adapter-exposed stubs, and there is no baseline, mutation study, variance or code. Use only the body numbers, and treat them as feasibility evidence from one model.
applicability: Indirect for the DAG question. If the Java team ever runs a declared agent graph (LangGraph or SDK handoffs among ingestion or spec agents), the cheap idea worth borrowing is per-edge regression checks: derive one obligation per declared edge and assert from traces that it was traversed and that no undeclared tool was called. The paper's more useful finding is negative. In LLM-routed handoff graphs the model does not reliably follow declared edges: about a quarter of delegations and almost a third of allowed-tool edges went unexercised, multi-hop routes were the hardest, and off-edge tool attempts occurred when tools were visible. That argues for authoring transitions in deterministic code (P36 with code-owned edges) and enforcing tool allowlists in the harness, rather than relying on role prompts. It is Python/OpenAI SDK only, not about coding tasks, and says nothing about Java or multi-repo work.

conflicts_with.detail: Agrees in direction: OpenCollab measures 47-97% adherence to declared collaboration topologies. Both papers find that LLM agents do not reliably execute the structure they are declared to follow.
